# Functional Components of a Computer
- A computer system consists of four major functional components: Input Unit, Central Processing Unit (CPU), Memory Unit, and Output Unit.
- The Input Unit accepts data and instructions from the user and converts them into a form that the computer can understand.
- Examples of Input Unit include keyboard, mouse, scanner, microphone, webcam, barcode reader, and touch screen.
- The Central Processing Unit (CPU) is known as the brain of the computer, performing data processing and controlling all operations.
- The CPU consists of three main components: Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU), Control Unit (CU), and Registers.
- The Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) performs arithmetic and logical operations.
- The Control Unit controls and coordinates the activities of all components of the computer.
- Registers are small storage locations inside the CPU used to hold data and instructions temporarily.
- The Memory Unit stores data, instructions, and results for future use, enabling the computer to retain information during and after processing.
- Primary Memory is directly accessible by the CPU, including Registers, Cache Memory, RAM, and ROM.
- The speed order of primary memory is: Registers → Cache Memory → RAM → ROM.
- Secondary Memory is used for permanent storage of data, including Hard Disk Drive (HDD), Solid State Drive (SSD), Pen Drive, Memory Card, CD, and DVD.
- The Output Unit presents processed information to the user in a human-readable form, converting machine-generated results into meaningful output.
- Examples of Output Unit include Monitor, Printer, Speaker, Projector, and Plotter.
- Primary Memory has limited storage capacity but is faster than Secondary Memory.
- Secondary Memory has a large storage capacity but is slower than Primary Memory.
- The CPU executes instructions and coordinates the activities of different units.

# Evolution of Computers
- The evolution of computers refers to the gradual development of computer technology.
- The development is from large, slow, and expensive machines to modern high-speed, compact, and intelligent systems.
- The evolution is generally divided into five generations based on the technology used.
- The generations are based on the technology used in the computers.
- The evolution shows an improvement in speed, size, and cost of computers.
- Modern computers are high-speed, compact, and intelligent systems.
- The evolution of computers is a gradual process.
- Computer technology has developed over time.
- The development of computers has led to smaller, faster, and more affordable machines.
- The five generations of computers are a way to categorize the evolution of computer technology.
- Each generation represents a significant improvement in computer technology.
- The evolution of computers has transformed the way people live and work.
- Computer technology has become an essential part of modern life.
- The development of computers has been a continuous process.
- The five generations provide a framework for understanding the evolution of computers.
- The evolution of computers has led to numerous advancements in technology.
- The improvements in computer technology have been significant.
- The evolution of computers is an important topic in the history of technology.
- The development of modern computers has revolutionized the way people communicate and work.

# Generations of Computers
- First Generation Computers (1940-1956) used vacuum tubes for processing and magnetic drums for memory.
- Characteristics of First Generation Computers: vacuum tube technology, large size, high power consumption, excessive heat generation, machine language programming, low reliability.
- Examples of First Generation Computers: ENIAC, EDVAC, UNIVAC I.
- Second Generation Computers (1956-1963) used transistors, which were smaller, faster, and more reliable.
- Characteristics of Second Generation Computers: transistor technology, smaller size, less heat generation, higher reliability, lower power consumption, faster processing speed.
- Examples of Second Generation Computers: IBM 1401, IBM 7094, CDC 1604.
- Third Generation Computers (1964-1971) used Integrated Circuits (ICs) with many transistors on a single silicon chip.
- Characteristics of Third Generation Computers: Integrated Circuit technology, smaller and more reliable, reduced maintenance, increased processing speed, lower power consumption, support for multiprogramming.
- Examples of Third Generation Computers: IBM System/360, PDP-8, IBM 370.
- Fourth Generation Computers (1971-Present) are based on microprocessors with a complete CPU on a single chip.
- Characteristics of Fourth Generation Computers: microprocessor technology, very high speed, compact size, large memory capacity, low cost, personal computer revolution.
- Examples of Fourth Generation Computers: IBM PC, Apple Macintosh, modern desktops and laptops.
- Fifth Generation Computers (Present and Beyond) are associated with Artificial Intelligence (AI) and machine learning.
- Characteristics of Fifth Generation Computers: Artificial Intelligence, machine learning, natural language processing, expert systems, robotics, intelligent automation.
- Examples of Fifth Generation Computers: AI-based systems, intelligent robots, voice assistants, advanced supercomputers.
- Key features of computer generations include technology, size, power consumption, heat generation, and programming language.
- Each generation of computers shows improvement in speed, reliability, and storage capacity.
- The development of computers has led to the growth of personal computers and modern computing systems.
- Artificial Intelligence is a key feature of Fifth Generation Computers.
- Machine learning and natural language processing are also important aspects of Fifth Generation Computers.

# Classification of Computers
- Computers can be classified on the basis of Data Handling, Purpose, and Size and Processing Power.
- Classification Based on Data Handling includes Analog, Digital, and Hybrid Computers.
- Analog Computers process continuous data, such as temperature, pressure, speed, and voltage.
- Examples of Analog Computers include Thermometer, Speedometer, and Analog Voltmeter.
- Digital Computers process discrete data represented in binary form (0 and 1).
- Examples of Digital Computers include Desktop Computer, Laptop, Smartphone, and Calculator.
- Hybrid Computers combine the features of both Analog and Digital Computers.
- Examples of Hybrid Computers include ECG Machines, ICU Monitoring Systems, and Weather Forecasting Systems.
- Classification Based on Purpose includes General Purpose and Special Purpose Computers.
- General Purpose Computers perform a variety of tasks, such as Desktop PCs, Laptops, and Tablets.
- Special Purpose Computers perform a specific task, such as ATM Machines, Traffic Control Systems, and Embedded Systems.
- Classification Based on Size and Processing Power includes Microcomputers, Minicomputers, Mainframe Computers, and Supercomputers.
- Microcomputers are small computers designed for individual users, such as Desktop, Laptop, Tablet, and Smartphone.
- Minicomputers are medium-sized computers capable of supporting multiple users simultaneously, used in small and medium-sized organizations.
- Mainframe Computers are large and powerful systems used to process huge volumes of data and support hundreds or thousands of users, used in Banks, Railways, Airlines, and Insurance Companies.
- Supercomputers are the fastest and most powerful computers.

# Applications of Computers
- Computers are used in almost every field of life due to their speed, accuracy, storage, automation, and efficient data processing.
- Education sector uses computers for online classes, computer-based examinations, digital libraries, and research activities.
- Business applications include accounting, payroll processing, inventory management, and business communication.
- Banking and finance applications include online banking, ATM services, fund transfers, and customer account management.
- Computers in healthcare are used for patient record management, medical diagnosis, laboratory testing, and medical imaging.
- Science and research applications include data analysis, scientific simulations, weather forecasting, and space research.
- Computers facilitate communication through email, video conferencing, social networking, and instant messaging.
- Entertainment applications include gaming, music and video streaming, animation, and movie production.
- Government organizations use computers for census data processing, tax administration, e-governance, and public record management.
- Industries use computers for process control, automation, robotics, quality control, and production planning.
- Transportation systems use computers for railway reservation, airline reservation, traffic management, and navigation systems.
- Defense and security applications include missile guidance systems, surveillance systems, and military communication.
- E-commerce enables online buying and selling of products and services through digital payments and online marketplaces.
- Computers are essential in various fields due to their speed, accuracy, reliability, and storage capabilities.
- Computers have become indispensable in modern society, transforming various sectors.
- Key applications of computers are found in education, business, banking, healthcare, research, and communication.
- Computers provide efficient data processing, making them valuable in every field.
- The use of computers improves productivity and efficiency in various sectors.
- Computers have transformed the way services are provided in banking, healthcare, and education.

# Input Devices
- Input devices enable users to enter data and commands into a computer.
- Keyboard is a widely used input device with keys for typing and functions, available in wireless form.
- Mouse is a pointing device used to control the cursor with buttons for selection and a sensor to track movement.
- Scanner scans documents, images, and other media, converting them into digital formats.
- Trackball is a stationary pointing device with a ball that controls the cursor, requiring less space than a mouse.
- Light Pen is a light-sensitive pen used to draw or select objects on a CRT screen.
- Microphone converts sound into electrical signals for speech recognition and voice commands.
- Optical Character Reader (OCR) scans printed or handwritten text, converting it into digital data.
- Bar Code Reader reads bar codes and converts them into digital data for processing.
- Joystick is used mainly for games and simulation applications.
- Touch Screen acts as both input and output device.
- MICR (Magnetic Ink Character Recognition) is used in banking to read cheque numbers.
- Input devices convert entered information into a format that the computer can process.
- Keyboard, mouse, and microphone are common input devices.
- Scanner and OCR are used for document and text conversion.
- Light Pen and Touch Screen provide direct interaction with the display.
- Bar Code Reader and MICR are used for specific applications like retail and banking.

# Output Devices
- Output devices convert digital information into visual, audio, or physical results.
- Monitor is an output device also called VDU (Visual Display Unit).
- Monitor displays information from the computer like text, video, images, etc.
- Printer is an output device that transfers data from the computer in a printed format.
- Types of printers include Impact Printers and Non-Impact Printers.
- Impact Printers include Dot Matrix Printer, Daisy Wheel Printer, and Line Printer.
- Non-Impact Printers include Inkjet Printer, Laser Printer, and Thermal Printer.
- Laser Printer uses laser technology and is faster and quieter than impact printers.
- Plotter is used to generate large drawings, architectural blueprints, etc. on paper.
- Speakers are output devices that give sound as an output.
- Soft Copy Output devices include Monitor and Projector.
- Hard Copy Output devices include Printer and Plotter.
- Output devices present processed data in a user-friendly form.
- Monitors are similar to TV screens.
- Printers can be colored or black & white.
- Plotters produce high-quality images and drawings.

# Memory Devices
- Storage devices, also known as secondary storage devices, store data and programs for long-term use.
- CD (Compact disc) is a circular storage medium with a storage capacity of about 600–700 MB.
- There are 3 types of CDs: CD-ROM, CD-R, and CD-RW.
- CD-ROM (CD - Read Only Memory) data cannot be erased or modified by users.
- CD-R (CD-Recordable) data can be written only once and read multiple times.
- CD-RW (CD-Rewritable) can rewrite content or erase previous content and write new content many times.
- DVD (Digital Video/Versatile Disc) offers higher storage capacity than CD, with single and dual-layer formats.
- A one-sided single-layer DVD stores about 4.7 GB, while a double-layer stores 8.5 GB.
- DVD types include DVD-ROM, DVD-R, DVD+R, DVD-RW, and DVD+RW.
- Hard Disk is a non-volatile storage device used for long-term data storage, storing digital information on magnetic surfaces.
- Hard Disk types include Internal Hard Disk, Internal Cartridges, and Hard Disk Packs.
- Internal Hard Disk is installed inside the system cabinet, offering high-speed performance.
- SSD (Solid State Drive) is a modern fast storage device using flash memory, offering higher speed and reliability.
- USB Drive is a modern portable storage device used to store and transfer data between computers using a USB interface.
- DVD-R and DVD+R are recordable discs that allow data to be written once and read many times.
- DVD-RW and DVD+RW are rewritable discs that can be erased and reused multiple times.
- DVD-RAM is a rewritable disc that functions similar to a hard disk, offering high data reliability.
- Hard Disk Packs are storage systems used by large organizations to handle large volumes of data.

# Software Concepts
- Software is a collection of programs, procedures, and related documentation that instructs a computer to perform specific tasks.
- Software acts as an interface between the user and the computer hardware.
- Characteristics of Software: intangible, consists of programs and instructions, controls and manages computer operations, enables communication between the user and hardware, can be modified, updated, and maintained.
- Software is broadly classified into two categories: System Software and Application Software.
- System Software manages and controls computer hardware and provides a platform for running application software.
- Functions of System Software: manages hardware resources, controls memory and processor operations, manages files and devices, provides security and user interface.
- Types of System Software: Operating System (OS), Device Drivers, Language Translators, Utility Software.
- Operating System (OS) examples: Microsoft Windows, Linux, Unix, macOS, Android.
- Application Software is designed to help users perform specific tasks.
- Functions of Application Software: solves user-specific problems, increases productivity, automates tasks, provides user-friendly interfaces.
- Types of Application Software: General-Purpose Application Software, Customized (Special-Purpose) Application Software.
- General-Purpose Application Software examples: MS Word, MS Excel, MS PowerPoint, Web Browsers.
- Customized (Special-Purpose) Application Software examples: Banking Software, Hospital Management System, Payroll System.
- Difference Between System Software and Application Software: System Software manages computer resources, Application Software performs user-specific tasks.
- Hardware and software are interdependent: hardware cannot function without software, software cannot run without hardware.

# Problem Solving Methodology
- Problem Solving Methodology is a systematic approach to identify, analyze, design, develop, and maintain solutions to a problem.
- Problem definition is the first step in problem solving, involving understanding objectives, requirements, inputs, outputs, and constraints.
- Problem analysis involves studying the problem to understand its nature and requirements, examining available data, processing requirements, and limitations.
- Solution design is represented using algorithms and flowcharts, with an algorithm being a finite sequence of well-defined steps.
- A flowchart is a graphical representation of an algorithm, using standard symbols to illustrate the sequence of operations.
- Program development involves converting the designed solution into a program using a programming language.
- Testing is the process of executing the program with different sets of input data to detect defects and ensure software meets specified requirements.
- Debugging is the process of locating, identifying, and removing errors from a program, including syntax, logical, and runtime errors.
- Implementation involves installing and deploying the software in the actual working environment.
- Documentation includes written information describing the software system, such as system design, program structure, and operation procedures.
- Maintenance is the process of modifying and updating software after deployment, with types including corrective, adaptive, perfective, and preventive maintenance.
- Corrective maintenance corrects defects, faults, and bugs discovered after software release.
- Adaptive maintenance modifies software to remain compatible with changes in its operating environment.
- Perfective maintenance improves software performance, efficiency, usability, or functionality based on user feedback and changing requirements.
- Preventive maintenance reduces the probability of future failures and improves software reliability.
- Problem Solving Methodology provides a disciplined approach for developing reliable, efficient, and maintainable software solutions.
- The methodology involves a series of steps, including problem definition, analysis, solution design, coding, testing, implementation, documentation, and maintenance.
- Good programming practices improve software quality and make future maintenance easier.
- Software maintenance is essential to remain useful and effective, as user requirements, business processes, and technologies change over time.

# Word Processing
- Word Processing is the use of a computer to create, edit, format, save, retrieve, and print documents.
- A Word Processor is software used for word processing, such as Microsoft Word, Google Docs, and LibreOffice Writer.
- Important features include Word Wrap, Spell Check, Grammar Check, AutoCorrect, and AutoText.
- Word Wrap automatically moves text to the next line when the current line is full.
- Spell Check detects spelling mistakes in a document, while Grammar Check detects grammatical errors.
- AutoCorrect automatically corrects common typing and spelling mistakes.
- AutoText stores frequently used text for quick insertion.
- Thesaurus provides synonyms and alternative words.
- Find and Replace are used to search and replace words throughout a document.
- Mail Merge creates multiple personalized documents using a Main Document, Data Source, and Merge Fields.
- Header and Footer display information at the top and bottom of every page, respectively.
- Page Number automatically numbers document pages.
- Template refers to a pre-designed document format.
- Print Preview shows the appearance of a document before printing.
- Hyperlink is a clickable link to a webpage, file, or location in a document.
- Key file extensions include .docx, .doc, .rtf, .txt, and .pdf.
- Important shortcut keys include Ctrl + N, Ctrl + O, Ctrl + S, Ctrl + P, and Ctrl + W for file operations.
- Editing operations shortcut keys include Ctrl + X, Ctrl + C, Ctrl + V, Ctrl + Z, and Ctrl + Y.
- Formatting operations shortcut keys include Ctrl + B, Ctrl + I, Ctrl + U, and Ctrl + Shift + > or < for font size.

# Spreadsheets
- A Spreadsheet is an electronic worksheet used to organize, calculate, analyze, and store data in rows and columns.
- Examples of spreadsheet applications include Microsoft Excel, Google Sheets, and LibreOffice Calc.
- A Workbook is a spreadsheet file containing one or more worksheets.
- A Worksheet is a single spreadsheet consisting of rows and columns.
- A Row is a horizontal arrangement of cells, identified by numbers.
- A Column is a vertical arrangement of cells, identified by letters.
- A Cell is the intersection of a row and a column, with a unique address.
- Every formula starts with "=".
- Functions include SUM(), AVERAGE(), MAX(), MIN(), and COUNT().
- SUM() is used for addition, AVERAGE() calculates mean value, MAX() returns highest value, MIN() returns lowest value, and COUNT() counts numeric cells.
- AutoSum shortcut is Alt + =, and F2 edits the active cell.
- F4 creates an absolute reference ($A$1).
- .xlsx is the default Excel file extension.
- A1:A10 represents a cell range.
- Sorting arranges data in ascending or descending order.
- Filtering displays selected records.
- Common chart types include Column Chart, Bar Chart, Line Chart, Pie Chart, and Area Chart.
- Ctrl + N creates a new workbook, Ctrl + O opens a workbook, and Ctrl + S saves a workbook.
- Important shortcut keys include Ctrl + C (copy), Ctrl + X (cut), Ctrl + V (paste), and Ctrl + Z (undo).

# PowerPoint Presentation
- Microsoft PowerPoint (MS PowerPoint) is a presentation software developed by Microsoft.
- A presentation is a collection of slides used to communicate information visually.
- A slide is a single page of a presentation.
- Slide Show is displaying slides sequentially on a screen.
- A placeholder is a predefined area in a slide used for text, images, charts, or other objects.
- Slide Layout refers to the arrangement of content on a slide.
- A theme is a predefined combination of colors, fonts, and effects applied to a presentation.
- A template is a pre-designed presentation format.
- Normal View is the default view used for creating and editing slides.
- Slide Sorter View displays all slides as thumbnails for easy arrangement.
- Animation is a visual effect applied to text or objects on a slide.
- Transition is a visual effect applied when moving from one slide to another.
- Ctrl + M inserts a new slide.
- Ctrl + D duplicates a slide.
- F5 starts Slide Show from the beginning.
- Shift + F5 starts Slide Show from the current slide.
- .pptx is the default PowerPoint file extension.
- Animation is applied to objects, while Transition is applied between slides.
- SmartArt is used for diagrams and visual representation, including processes, hierarchies, relationships, and cycles.

# Typical Configuration of Computer System
- A Typical Computer System Configuration includes input devices, processing unit, memory, storage devices, output devices, and supporting components.
- The Input Unit converts user input into a machine-readable form and sends it to the CPU for processing.
- Common Input Devices include Keyboard, Mouse, Scanner, Microphone, Webcam, and Barcode Reader.
- The Central Processing Unit (CPU) is the brain of the computer, performing data processing, executing instructions, and controlling all computer operations.
- The CPU consists of Control Unit (CU), Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU), and Registers.
- The Control Unit (CU) controls and coordinates all activities of the computer and manages the flow of data between different units.
- The Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) performs arithmetic and logical operations.
- Registers are high-speed storage locations inside the CPU and are the fastest memory in a computer system.
- The Memory Unit stores data, instructions, and results, and includes Primary Memory and Secondary Memory.
- Primary Memory is directly accessed by the CPU and includes Registers, Cache Memory, RAM, and ROM.
- Secondary Memory provides permanent storage of data and includes Hard Disk Drive (HDD), Solid State Drive (SSD), Pen Drive, and Memory Card.
- The speed order of memory is Registers → Cache Memory → RAM → ROM.
- Common Output Devices include Monitor, Printer, Speaker, Plotter, and Projector.
- Storage devices include HDD, SSD, USB Flash Drive, Optical Disks, and External Hard Drives.
- The Motherboard is the main circuit board of a computer, connecting all components.
- The Power Supply Unit (PSU) converts AC power into DC power and supplies electricity to all components.
- A standard desktop computer configuration includes CPU, Motherboard, RAM, Storage Device, Keyboard, Mouse, Monitor, Printer, Speakers, and Power Supply Unit.

# Introduction to Motherboard
- The Motherboard is the main circuit board of a computer, also known as the System Board, Main Board, or Logic Board.
- It connects and coordinates all hardware components such as the CPU, memory, storage devices, input devices, and output devices.
- A motherboard provides electrical connections and communication pathways for different components to interact efficiently.
- It is considered one of the most important components of a computer as all major hardware devices are directly or indirectly connected to it.
- The motherboard's functions include connecting hardware components, providing communication between CPU, memory, and peripherals, and distributing power.
- It houses system firmware (BIOS/UEFI) and supports expansion cards and additional devices.
- The motherboard controls data transfer among connected components.
- Major components of a motherboard include the CPU Socket, Memory Slots (RAM Slots), Chipset, and BIOS / UEFI Chip.
- The CPU socket provides physical and electrical connection between the CPU and the motherboard.
- Memory slots are used to install RAM modules for temporary working memory.
- The chipset manages communication between the processor, memory, storage devices, and peripherals.
- Expansion slots are used to add extra capabilities such as graphics, sound, and network cards.
- Storage connectors like SATA Ports and M.2 Slots connect storage devices to the motherboard.
- The power connector supplies electrical power from the Power Supply Unit (PSU) to the motherboard.
- Input/Output ports like USB, HDMI, Ethernet, and Audio ports allow external devices to connect to the computer.
- The advantages of a motherboard include enabling communication between components, supporting hardware upgrades, providing centralized control, and ensuring efficient data transfer.
- A motherboard supports hardware upgrades and expansion through its various components and slots.
- It provides a centralized control of hardware devices, ensuring efficient operation of the computer system.

# Types of Motherboards
- A motherboard can be classified based on its form factor, which defines its size, layout, mounting points, and compatibility with computer cases.
- Important motherboard types for competitive examinations are AT, ATX, Micro-ATX, Mini-ITX, and BTX.
- AT (Advanced Technology) Motherboard is an older motherboard standard, largely replaced by ATX.
- AT motherboards have large size, older technology, manual power switches, and are difficult to upgrade and maintain.
- ATX (Advanced Technology Extended) Motherboard is the most commonly used motherboard form factor in desktop computers.
- ATX motherboards have better component arrangement, improved airflow and cooling, and support modern processors and expansion cards.
- Micro-ATX Motherboard is a smaller version of the ATX motherboard with fewer expansion slots and lower cost.
- Micro-ATX provides ATX functionality in a smaller size, suitable for home and office computers.
- Mini-ITX Motherboard is a compact motherboard with very small size, low power consumption, and is suitable for compact PCs.
- Mini-ITX is popular for Small Form Factor (SFF) computers and commonly used in embedded systems and mini computers.
- BTX (Balanced Technology Extended) Motherboard was developed to improve cooling and system performance but was not widely adopted.
- BTX motherboards have improved airflow design and better thermal management.
- Motherboards can be classified based on usage: Desktop, Laptop, Server, and Embedded.
- Desktop Motherboard is designed for personal desktop computers.
- Laptop Motherboard is compact and customized for specific laptop models.
- Server Motherboard supports multiple processors, has large memory capacity, high reliability, and continuous operation.
- Embedded Motherboard is used in dedicated systems such as ATMs, medical equipment, and industrial controllers.
- ATX is the most widely used motherboard type.
- AT is an older motherboard standard.

# Components of Motherboard
- The CPU Socket provides mechanical support and electrical connections between the CPU and the motherboard.
- RAM slots are used to install memory modules (RAM) and are also known as DIMM slots.
- The Chipset controls communication between the CPU, RAM, storage devices, and other peripherals.
- BIOS (Basic Input/Output System) or UEFI firmware is stored on a chip located on the motherboard.
- The CMOS battery provides power to store BIOS settings, date, and time even when the computer is switched off.
- Expansion slots are used to add additional cards to the computer, including PCI and PCIe slots.
- Graphics cards are commonly installed in PCIe slots.
- Storage connectors include SATA ports and M.2 slots, used for HDD, SSD, and optical drives.
- The Power Connector supplies power to the motherboard and connected devices.
- USB headers connect front-panel USB ports of the computer cabinet to the motherboard.
- I/O Ports, located on the rear panel, include USB, HDMI, VGA, Ethernet, and Audio ports.
- The Audio Chip provides onboard sound functionality, responsible for audio input and output.
- The Network Interface Controller (NIC) enables communication through LAN/Ethernet.
- A Heat Sink helps dissipate heat generated by components such as the CPU and chipset.
- Fan connectors provide power to CPU and cabinet cooling fans for cooling system management.
- The processor is mounted on the CPU Socket.
- RAM is installed in DIMM slots on the motherboard.
- The chipset acts as a traffic controller of the motherboard.
- BIOS is firmware stored on the motherboard.
- Modern NVMe SSDs use M.2 slots.

# Memory
- Memory is the storage unit of a computer that stores data, instructions, and information.
- Classification of Memory: Primary Memory and Secondary Memory.
- Primary Memory is directly accessible by the CPU and stores data and instructions currently being processed.
- Characteristics of Primary Memory: directly accessed by CPU, faster than secondary memory, limited storage capacity, expensive.
- Types of Primary Memory: Registers, Cache Memory, RAM, ROM.
- Registers are the fastest memory in a computer, used to store data and instructions temporarily.
- Cache Memory is a small, high-speed memory located between CPU and RAM, storing frequently used data and instructions.
- RAM is a volatile memory used to store programs and data currently being used by the computer.
- Characteristics of RAM: read and write memory, volatile, data lost when power is turned off.
- Types of RAM: SRAM, DRAM.
- ROM is non-volatile memory used to store permanent instructions, characteristics: non-volatile, permanent storage.
- Types of ROM: PROM, EPROM, EEPROM.
- Memory Hierarchy: Registers → Cache Memory → RAM → ROM.
- Secondary Memory is used for permanent storage of data and programs, characteristics: non-volatile, large storage capacity, slower than primary memory.
- Examples of Secondary Memory: Hard Disk Drive, Solid State Drive, Pen Drive, Memory Card, CD, DVD, Blu-ray Disc.
- Virtual Memory is a memory management technique that increases the effective memory capacity of a system.
- Comparison: RAM (volatile, read and write) vs ROM (non-volatile, mostly read-only).

# Power Supply to the Computer System
- The Power Supply Unit (PSU) converts Alternating Current (AC) into Direct Current (DC) for computer components.
- The PSU supplies power to the motherboard, processor, memory, storage devices, and other peripheral components.
- Functions of PSU: converts AC to DC, supplies power to motherboard, regulates voltage, and protects from power fluctuations.
- Main components powered by PSU: Motherboard, Processor, Hard Disk Drive, Solid State Drive, Optical Drives, Graphics Card, and Cooling Fans.
- Types of Power Supply: AT Power Supply (obsolete) and ATX Power Supply (most commonly used).
- ATX Power Supply features: better power management, automatic shutdown support, improved efficiency, and supports modern hardware.
- Power Rating is measured in Watts (W), with common ratings including 450W, 550W, 650W, 750W, and 850W.
- Higher-performance computers require higher wattage power supplies.
- SMPS (Switched Mode Power Supply) is used in modern computers for efficient AC to DC conversion.
- Advantages of SMPS: high efficiency, compact size, low heat generation, lightweight, and reliable operation.
- Important Terms: AC (Alternating Current), DC (Direct Current), Watt (W), and UPS (Uninterruptible Power Supply).
- UPS functions: prevents sudden shutdowns, protects data, protects hardware, and provides backup power.
- UPS provides temporary power when the main electricity supply fails.
- The Power Supply Unit is essential for computer operation as all internal components require electrical power.
- ATX is the standard PSU used in modern computers.
- The power supply used in modern computers is called SMPS.
- PSU regulates voltage to ensure stable operation and protects the system from overload conditions.
- PSU distributes power to various components through different connectors.

# Assembling the Computer System
- Assembling a computer system involves connecting and installing hardware components for efficient performance, reliability, and ease of maintenance.
- Components required for assembly include Computer Cabinet, Motherboard, Processor, RAM, Hard Disk Drive or Solid State Drive, Power Supply Unit, and necessary cables.
- The first step in assembling a computer is to install the Switched Mode Power Supply (SMPS) inside the computer cabinet.
- The motherboard is mounted securely inside the cabinet using screws and spacers.
- The processor is carefully placed into the CPU socket on the motherboard with proper alignment.
- A heat sink and cooling fan are installed on top of the processor to dissipate heat.
- RAM modules are inserted into the memory slots (DIMM slots) of the motherboard.
- Storage devices like HDDs and SSDs are mounted in drive bays and connected to the motherboard using SATA or M.2 interfaces.
- Power cables from the SMPS are connected to the motherboard, processor, HDD/SSD, and other components.
- Expansion cards such as graphics cards are installed in PCIe slots.
- Front panel cables are connected to the motherboard, including power switch, reset switch, and LEDs.
- External peripherals like monitor, keyboard, and mouse are connected to the system.
- After assembly, the system is checked for proper connections and powered on for testing.
- Post-assembly tasks include verifying BIOS/UEFI detection of hardware, checking CPU temperature, and installing the operating system and device drivers.
- Important precautions during assembly include switching off power, using anti-static precautions, and handling components carefully.
- The motherboard serves as the main circuit board connecting all components.
- SATA cables are used to connect HDDs and SSDs to the motherboard.
- PCIe slots are commonly used for graphics cards.
